uncited: This family encompasses numerical methods for discretizing and solving the Navier-Stokes equations to simulate incompressible fluid flow, producing velocity and pressure fields for volumetric rendering [13501-navier-stokes-solver-components.md].
It solves the problem of computing physically plausible fluid motion from continuous partial differential equations into a discrete grid-based representation.

It is distinguished from particle-based methods (like [Position Based Fluids](1765-position-based-fluids.md)) by its Eulerian grid-based approach, and from pure advection methods (like [Smoke Advection](4639-smoke-advection.md)) by its inclusion of pressure projection and diffusion steps required to maintain incompressibility and viscosity [13501-navier-stokes-solver-components.md].
All methods in this family solve the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on a staggered or collocated grid.
**Velocity Advection**: Advecting the velocity field $\mathbf{u}$ by itself using the convective term $(\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla) \mathbf{u}$ [13501-navier-stokes-solver-components.md].
**Pressure Projection**: Solving a Poisson equation for pressure $p$ to enforce the divergence-free constraint ($\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0$) [13501-navier-stokes-solver-components.md].

**Diffusion**: Solving a diffusion equation for viscosity $
u$ to handle viscous forces $

abla^2 \mathbf{u}$ [13501-navier-stokes-solver-components.md].

**Time Integration**: Advancing the state using a semi-Lagrangian or similar scheme, typically splitting the operations into advection, diffusion, and pressure solve steps per time step $dt$ [13501-navier-stokes-solver-components.md].
The Navier-Stokes equations, formulated in the 19th century, describe the motion of viscous fluid substances.

In computer graphics, their application to fluid simulation was pioneered by Jos Stam in 1999 with "Stable Fluids," which introduced semi-Lagrangian advection and stable integration schemes suitable for real-time rendering .
This work laid the foundation for grid-based fluid simulation in visual effects and games.
The family has since expanded to include specialized variants for fire and smoke, integrating thermal buoyancy and density transport .
